items.title: Land Acknowledgement

Chair J. Erb provided a land acknowledgement. 

Chair J. Erb also provided a brief background on the 2026 Black History Month GRT bus wrap and provided an overview of the accomplishments and scope of work that artist Vanessa Nkansah-Okoree has achieved.

items.title: Declarations of Pecuniary Interest under the “Municipal Conflict of Interest Act”
David Alton, Social Development Centre Waterloo Region
notes:
D. Alton provided an overview of a proposed safe tenting framework and public camping by-law, and reviewed community engagement efforts that the Social Development Centre has undertaken. 

In response to questions from the Committee, D. Alton clarified that a safe tenting framework is intended to provide an option of last resort for individuals who are unhoused, not serve as a replacement or preferred alternative to supportive and affordable housing options.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Equitable Services and Opportunities
PHP-SPS-26-001, Collaborative Approach to Addressing Substance Use and Addictions
notes:
Dr. Wang provided an introduction to the report, noting that substance use issues are complex and require a multi-component response that includes community agencies, grassroots organizations, municipalities, and public health to make meaningful progress.

Katie McDonald, Manager, Health System Integration and Strategic Partnerships, highlighted statistics and key indicators for opioid use and overdoses in the Region, noting that these trends could change at any time, but that they are currently trending downward.

Tara Groves-Taylor, Chief Executive Officer, Community Health Caring and HART Hub Co-lead, noted that the Region's HART Hub services are currently 96% operational, but are projected to reach 100% in March once the transitional housing program becomes operational. She highlighted that to date, the HART Hub has had just under 3,000 service interactions with individuals seeking support, and that next steps include expanding integrated health, social, and addictions supports across the Region.

Anne Phillips, Senior Director, Sanguen Health Centre, provided an overview of harm reduction efforts in Waterloo Region, noting the work of community partners and highlighting 2025 harm reduction successes as well as opportunities for next steps.

K. McDonald noted that Public Health will continue to work with community partners to engage in a muli-sector approach to addressing addictions and substance use in Waterloo Region.

In response to the Committee, T. Groves-Taylor explained that one of the challenges the HART Hub will face when the 12-bed transitional housing program becomes operational is a lack of supportive housing options for program participants to transition into once they are ready to leave the transitional housing program, noting that supportive housing spaces exist within the Region but that they lack operational funding.

A. Phillips noted that future funding opportunities from the provincial government are unclear, and that advocacy from Regional Council to the province to secure funding to provide a full spectrum of services related to addictions and substance use would be helpful.

K. McDonald and Monica Vythilingam, Epidemiologist, clarified that the provided statistics surrounding opioid-related deaths include both suspected and confirmed overdose deaths. Dr. Wang noted that suspected opioid-related deaths are later confirmed by the Coroner's Office, but that both suspected and confirmed opioid-related deaths are tracked and monitored year-over-year.

T. Groves-Taylor confirmed that funding from the provincial government can be used retroactively for HART Hub's transitional housing program, noting that House of Friendship had already begun work on establishing the transitional housing program before provincial funding had been received. She also confirmed that HART Hub will be provincially funded for five years.

K. McDonald confirmed that the majority of overdose deaths occur in private residences. She also noted that it is difficult to obtain exact numbers of community members using drugs in the Region, but that other statistics such as the number of needle syringe program clients can provide rough estimates on the number of individuals using drugs.

Dr. Wang explained that several factors can contribute to decreases in opioid-related deaths, including reduced toxicity levels in drug supply, increased access to naloxone, and a decreased number of individuals at risk of opioid-related deaths. 

K. McDonald confirmed that the most common age range for opioid-related incidents is the 25-44 age bracket, noting that further information and statistics are available on the Public Health online dashboard. 

John Riches, Chief, Paramedic Services, confirmed that there is not currently an alternate destination clinic in the Region but that his team is working to establish a framework with which to apply to the province for approval for alternate destination patient care.

In response to the Committee, K. McDonald confirmed that overdoses that are reversed within the community and thus not reported may not necessarily be captured in Public Health overdose statistics.

Received for information.

items.title: PHP-CFH-26-001, Youth Substance Use Prevention
notes:
Jonathan Mall, Manager, Substance Use Prevention, provided an overview of upstream initiatives in place to prevent youth substance use and address mental health issues, highlighting current youth substance use statistics in Waterloo Region and noting that youth substance use is slightly higher in the Region than the provincial average. J. Mall also discussed the link between youth mental health and substance use and noted several services provided by Public Health to support healthy childhood development.

Alison Pearson, Manager, Children and Youth Planning Table, and Pamela Fehr, Consultant to the Lead Agency for Child and Youth Mental Health, provided an update on the recent work of the Children and Youth Planning Table, noting that a primary focus right now is to ensure that children and youth feel a sense of belonging within their communities and to work with community partners to advance prevention strategies for youth mental health and addictions.

Dave Cooke, Director of Community Services at the Youth Wellness Hub Ontario, Cambridge and Langs, provided an overview of the new Youth Wellness Hub in Cambridge and the integrated youth services it provides, including mental health and substance use supports and primary health care.

P. Fehr noted that Starling Community Services is designated as the lead agency for children and youth mental health in the Region and works collaboratively with other community partners to plan and deliver services.

In response to the Committee, J. Mall clarified that in order to better understand why Region of Waterloo youth have higher rates of substance use than the provincial average, further in-depth research would be required. Dr. Wang also noted that these statistics should be interpreted with caution due to wide confidence intervals for the data, but that Public Health will continue monitoring these statistics and that improved data analysis will support better understanding of youth substance use trends.

J. Mall also confirmed that Public Health partners with school boards to educate on youth substance use and available youth programs and supports. 

D. Cooke confirmed that youth can be referred to Youth Wellness Hubs but that youth crisis services are not offered, however, youth arriving in crisis are served by clinicians on site who ensure their safety before connecting youth with community partner organizations that are able to provide crisis services.

P. Fehr emphasized that current youth strategies strive to meet children and youth needs in a way that is tailored to each specific set of circumstances and uses the appropriate community partner agencies to do so rather than relying exclusively on the traditional model of healthcare service delivery.

J. Mall also confirmed that partnerships exist with post-secondary institutions and that programming is provided for youth up to 25 years of age. 

In response to the Committee, J. Mall also confirmed that as part of interactions with secondary institutions, Public Health engages with parents and provides education to parents on youth substance use and available supports. P. Fehr also noted that parent information sessions are available at Youth Wellness Hubs, and that projects are underway with community partners to provide culturally relevant and appropriate education to families about mental health. 

D. Cooke confirmed that Youth Wellness Hub Cambridge continues to engage in advocacy work for additional Youth Wellness Hub sites to be introduced in the Region.

Received for information.

items.title: Other Business
notes: In response to the Committee, Peter Sweeney, Commissioner, Community Services, provided an update on warming centres, confirming that warming centres are open seven days a week rather than exclusively during extreme weather warnings. He also provided a brief overview of the surge protocols in place for funded community partners that provide emergency shelter, noting that the protocols allow them to respond quickly to extreme weather events without waiting for Regional approval to secure additional resources.
